item.title: BB paves way for PayPal, international payment services launch
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has paved the way to launch international digital payment and money transfer services, including PayPal and Payoneer, in the country.
Under a new policy framework, domestic banks can now partner with foreign digital payment service providers to facilitate cross-border digital transactions.
The central bank's Foreign Exchange Policy Department issued a circular regarding the matter on Wednesday (July 29).
The new structure has been introduced to simplify international service trade, expand digital financial inclusion, and modernize as well as streamline the country's foreign transaction systems.
The new guidelines introduce a "Bank-Intermediated Framework." Under this arrangement, local banks can offer services through partnerships with foreign digital payment service providers, online payment gateways, digital platforms, and other legitimate international payment solution providers.
According to the directive, banks will facilitate the opening of digital wallets or stored-value accounts known as "Digital Value Accounts (DVA)" for customers.
However, these accounts will not operate independently. Each DVA will be linked to a central "Master DVA" or settlement account managed directly by the respective bank.
To ensure transaction transparency and security, banks must maintain separate ledger records and implement real-time monitoring systems.
Any unused funds will remain under the bank's control and must be refunded or adjusted in accordance with prevailing regulations.
Under the new framework, individuals, businesses, and freelancers can execute various foreign currency transactions.
Foreign currency can be utilized within permissible travel quotas for personal, medical, or official trips abroad.
Additionally, users can spend up to $300 per transaction for small-scale online international purchases or fee payments.
The digital wallets can also be used to pay membership fees, IT-related expenses, visa processing fees, and online hotel bookings.
This facility can be utilized against Export Retention Quota (ERQ) and Resident Foreign Currency Deposit (RFCD) accounts.
Up to three top executives of an ERQ account-holding institution will be permitted to use DVAs for official business expenses.
Furthermore, freelancers and e-commerce entrepreneurs will be able to repatriate their foreign earnings more easily, which is expected to boost foreign exchange inflows.
Foreign nationals and tourists visiting Bangladesh will also be able to make digital payments at local merchant points using this system.
Before rolling out these services, participating banks must submit detailed technical specifications, security infrastructure plans, and operational framework details to Bangladesh Bank's Foreign Exchange Policy Department to secure prior approval.
Banks must also strictly adhere to all Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Know Your Customer (KYC), and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) regulations, alongside submitting regular transaction reports to the central bank.

NCP leaders, police scuffle as convoy stopped in Sreemangal
item.description:
Saiful Islam
Police stopped the convoy of National Citizen Party (NCP) leaders in Sreemangal on Wednesday afternoon as they were heading to Habiganj to join a previously announced protest program, triggering a brief scuffle over police barricades.
The confrontation took place around 4:30pm near the Tea Maiden (Cha Kanya) sculpture on the Sreemangal-Shayestaganj road after police blocked the route with trucks and barricades.
NCP Convener Nahid Islam, Chief Organizer (Northern Region) Sarjis Alam, Chief Organizer (Southern Region) and MP Hasnat Abdullah, Chief Coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary and MP Dr Mahmuda Mitu got out of their vehicles and held talks with police officials at the scene.
At one stage, pushing and shoving broke out between police personnel and NCP leaders and activists. Hasnat Abdullah and Nasiruddin Patwary were seen in a scuffle with police as officers attempted to move them away from the barricade.
During an exchange with police, Hasnat questioned the legality of the blockade.
“If you can, provide us with security. If not, we will proceed at our own responsibility. Under what law are you stopping us?” he said.
Police officials cited security concerns, but Hasnat replied: “Who are the security threats? Instead of arresting them, you are blocking our road. You imposed Section 144 in Habiganj and are stopping us in Sreemangal. This is illegal.”
A police officer at the scene told the NCP leaders that “a major incident” could occur if they crossed the barricade.
The NCP convoy later crossed the barricade and resumed its journey to Habiganj.
According to party sources, Nahid, Opposition Chief Whip in parliament; Member Secretary Akhtar Hossain; Sarjis; Hasnat; Nasiruddin; Dr Mahmuda Mitu and other leaders left the Moulvibazar Circuit House for Habiganj around 3pm.
Police later set up barricades using trucks near the Tea Maiden sculpture, halting the convoy and causing traffic congestion, with hundreds of vehicles stranded on both sides of the road.
Moulvibazar Assistant Superintendent of Police (Sreemangal Circle) Md Wahiduzzaman Raju said the leaders had been stopped for security reasons.
The latest incident came a day after NCP leaders alleged that activists of the BNP, Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal and Jubo Dal attacked their convoy in Habiganj town following Tuesday’s program, leaving several people injured.
Amid heightened tensions between the BNP and the NCP, the administration-imposed Section 144 in the Habiganj municipal area from Wednesday morning.
Local sources said Chhatra Dal activists allegedly attacked vehicles carrying NCP leaders near Habiganj Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Several vehicles belonging to journalists were also vandalized.
Sarjis Alam and Nasiruddin Patwary reportedly took shelter in a branch of Sonali Bank during the attack before police escorted them to safety.
The NCP later suspended two previously announced “July March” programs in Moulvibazar and instead announced a protest rally in Habiganj, while separate programs by BNP and Chhatra Dal further heightened tensions in the district.

item.title: Trivedi: PM Tarique's India visit key to positive progress
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Wednesday expressed optimism about the future of bilateral ties, saying Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's proposed visit to India would pave the way for progress on outstanding issues, including the renewal of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty.
Speaking to reporters after separate courtesy meetings with Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Trivedi said discussions covered a range of issues and were held in a positive atmosphere.
"Once Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to India is confirmed and the joint working group sits down with the necessary documents, everything will move in a positive direction," he said.
The envoy said there was no bilateral issue that could not be resolved through dialogue in a way that served the mutual interests of both countries.
"There is no problem that cannot be resolved if it benefits both countries," he said.
On the renewal of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, Trivedi said the joint working group of the two countries was already discussing the matter.
"I hope they will meet soon. There is no issue that cannot be resolved. Whatever is necessary in the interests of the people of both countries will be done," he said.
Describing the meetings as constructive, the Indian high commissioner said the discussions focused on issues important to the people of both countries.
"At the end of the day, this is about the people of the two countries. Whatever is necessary for the democracies of both countries, those interests will be taken into consideration," he added.

item.title: Unified taxpayer data: IMF hands NBR new automation roadmap
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has recommended major structural reforms to Bangladesh’s revenue administration.
The global lender advised replacing separate identification numbers for income tax and Value Added Tax (VAT) with a single Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN).
The unified system would allow an individual or institution’s income tax, VAT, customs, import-export data, tax deduction at source (TDS), and other financial records to be viewed and analyzed on a single platform.
According to the IMF, the reform would enhance transparency and efficiency in tax administration, make tax evasion easier to detect, and ensure faster, more effective services for taxpayers.
The recommendation was made on Tuesday (July 28) during a special meeting between an IMF delegation and senior officials from the National Board of Revenue (NBR), including chairman Ahsan Habib and top heads of the tax and customs wings. Multiple sources present at the meeting confirmed the development.
Currently, Bangladesh uses an electronic Tax Identification Number (e-TIN) for income taxpayers and a Business Identification Number (BIN) for VAT-registered entities.
The IMF noted that having two separate identification numbers scatters a taxpayer’s data across different databases.
Consequently, a taxpayer’s complete economic activity cannot be monitored from one place, making effective data analysis difficult.
The IMF believes that establishing a single taxpayer identification system would centralize all relevant data under one number.
A taxpayer’s income tax returns, VAT filings, import-export details, TDS records, banking transactions, and other tax-related information could then be analyzed on a unified platform.
This would streamline risk-based audits, accelerate the detection of tax evasion, and significantly boost the efficiency of the tax administration.
During the meeting, IMF representatives highlighted that one of the NBR’s major limitations is storing income tax, VAT, and customs data in separate databases.
As a result, integrated analysis of a single taxpayer’s information remains impossible.
Implementing an integrated taxpayer identification framework would render data verification, risk assessment, and tax collection operations far more effective.
The move would also benefit taxpayers by eliminating the need to use multiple numbers for different services, allowing them to access all tax-related services using a single identification number.
Beyond recommending a single taxpayer number, the IMF emphasized the complete digital transformation of the revenue administration.
The organization recommended automatically linking the NBR’s central database with various government agencies, including the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (Bida), the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC), Bangladesh Bank, the Land Registration Authority, the Office of the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Bangladesh Customs, and the Ministry of Commerce.
This inter-agency connectivity would easily track the actual economic activities of taxable individuals and businesses.
Additionally, the IMF stressed the importance of data-driven compliance management, risk-based auditing, online income tax return filing, e-payments, and fully digitizing tax deduction at source (TDS) reporting.
According to the IMF, numerous countries have already adopted a unified taxpayer identification framework.
Examples include India’s Permanent Account Number (PAN), Nepal’s PAN, Hong Kong’s Business Registration Number (BRN), Singapore’s Unique Entity Number (UEN), Australia’s Australian Business Number (ABN), and New Zealand’s IRD number.
Prof Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), stated that introducing a single taxpayer identification number would benefit both the tax administration and taxpayers.
"If various registrations, tax deductions, business operations, and income tax data can be consolidated under a single number, the NBR’s coordination capacity will expand, minimizing opportunities for tax evasion. At the same time, taxpayers can access all necessary services using just one number," Prof. Rahman said.
He added that the initiative would play a positive role in boosting revenue collection, ensuring transparency in tax management, and driving the digital transformation of public services.
NBR’s preparedness
Several NBR officials mentioned that various reform initiatives are already underway to modernize revenue administration.
Automation, data integration, and full digitalization of taxpayer services are prioritized in the medium- and long-term revenue strategies.
According to NBR officials, the IMF has been recommending the unification of separate income tax and VAT identification numbers since 2005.
However, immediate implementation poses challenges under Bangladesh’s current reality.
The tax and VAT networks must first expand further, databases need integration, and technological infrastructure must be strengthened before considering a phased rollout of a single taxpayer identification system.
A fact-finding team led by Iva Petrova, the IMF’s Mission Chief for Bangladesh, is currently visiting the country.
The delegation is holding a series of discussions with the government on revenue administration reform, revenue mobilization, digital modernization, and broader economic reforms.

IPC: Over 15.3 million Bangladeshis face acute food insecurity
item.description:
More than 15.3 million people in Bangladesh are facing acute food insecurity, with the number projected to rise to 18.1 million by the end of 2026, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis.
The findings were presented at a high-level workshop in Dhaka organized by the Ministry of Food through its Food Planning and Monitoring Unit (FPMU), in collaboration with the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the UN World Food Programme (WFP), Action Against Hunger, Save the Children and the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN).
The workshop brought together senior government officials, representatives of development and humanitarian organizations, academics and civil society members to review the findings on July 13, according to a press release on Wednesday.
The analysis found that around 15% of the assessed population—equivalent to 15.3 million people—faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between May and August 2026. Of them, about 483,000 were classified under IPC Phase 4, indicating emergency levels of food insecurity.
The situation is expected to worsen between September and December, with the number of people facing acute food insecurity projected to increase to 18.1 million. Nearly 787,000 people are forecast to face emergency levels of food insecurity during the period.
The analysis identified the Chittagong Hill Tracts, the haor region, several coastal districts, and the Rohingya camps in Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char as the areas most vulnerable to food insecurity.
State Minister for Food Md Abdul Bari said the government places the highest importance on evidence-based analysis to strengthen food security and build resilience against future crises.
"The IPC findings will help improve the targeting of resources and strengthen coordinated interventions for vulnerable communities facing climate and economic pressures," he said.
Food Secretary Abu Taher Md Masud Rana said data-driven decision-making remains essential for effective policymaking.
He said the IPC findings would serve as an important guide for policymakers, development partners and humanitarian agencies in designing targeted programmes, strengthening food and nutrition security, and enhancing disaster resilience.
Director General of the NGO Affairs Bureau Dr Mohammad Zakaria stressed the need for stronger collaboration among the government, development partners, NGOs, UN agencies, research institutions and other stakeholders to address food insecurity.
The report attributed the worsening food insecurity to adverse weather, recurring floods, inflation, rising food and fuel prices, global supply chain disruptions and broader economic pressures, which have eroded purchasing power and made access to adequate and nutritious food increasingly difficult.
Participants at the workshop called for expanding life-saving food assistance, strengthening shock-responsive social protection, investing in climate-resilient agriculture, restoring livelihoods, and improving disaster preparedness and early warning systems.
FAO Representative in Bangladesh Dr Jiaoqun Shi said the findings underscored the urgent need to strengthen agriculture and food systems in areas repeatedly affected by floods, cyclones and other climate-related disasters.
"Investing in climate-resilient agriculture, sustainable livelihoods and local food production is critical not only for addressing today's food insecurity but also for protecting vulnerable communities against future crises," he said.
WFP Representative and Country Director in Bangladesh Coco Ushiyama said one of the key strengths of the IPC analysis is its ability to identify populations most at risk before conditions deteriorate.
She said many of the areas highlighted in the report are already experiencing heavy rainfall and flooding, particularly the Chittagong Hill Tracts, where WFP has activated anticipatory assistance while supporting the government's shock-responsive social protection initiatives.
Ushiyama added that the IPC analysis also plays a vital role in improving preparedness, enabling more effective humanitarian responses and strengthening community resilience against future shocks.
The Ministry of Food and its partners reaffirmed their commitment to working together to address immediate food needs, strengthen resilience to future disasters and ensure sustainable food security for all.

item.title: Law minister: Govt taken effective initiatives to reduce civil case backlog
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Wednesday said the present government has taken effective initiatives to reduce longstanding civil case backlog.
"Various reform initiatives are being implemented to make the judicial process faster, more efficient and more people-friendly. Backlog of cases could be reduced and the efficiency of the judicial process enhanced through the exchange of domestic and international experiences and mutual cooperation," he said.
The minister made the remarks at a seminar titled "Addressing Delays in the Disposal of Civil Cases: Shared Experiences of Bangladesh and Japan" at Judicial Administration Training Institute (JATI). Law and Justice Division and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) jointly organized the seminar, an official release said on Wednesday.
Md Asaduzzaman said that many civil cases in Bangladesh are still pending despite having remained unresolved for many years. The prolonged pendency of these cases has increased the sufferings of litigants and placed an additional burden on the judicial system, he added.
"To address this situation, the government is implementing various reform initiatives, including modernizing the judiciary, expanding Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), introducing technology-driven judicial services, and making the judicial process simpler and more efficient," he further said.
The law minister also said the experiences and cooperation of the Japanese Ministry of Justice and international partners, including the JICA, would play a significant role in strengthening Bangladesh's judicial system.
"Such joint initiatives would create new opportunities for the exchange of knowledge and experiences between the two countries, which would make a positive contribution to enhancing the efficiency of the judicial process," he added.
Speaking as the special guest, Deputy Director-General of the International Cooperation Department of Japan's Ministry of Justice, Kazunori Nose, assured that Japan would continue its cooperation in strengthening and enhancing the capacity of Bangladesh's judicial system.
The keynote papers were presented by Senior Assistant Secretary of the Law and Justice Division Syed Md Shafayet and Professor Wakazono Rei of Japan's Ministry of Justice. Project Director of the relevant project and Additional Secretary of the Law and Justice Division Md Khadem Ul Kayes chaired the seminar.

item.title: Health officials report 534 fresh cases of dengue inflection, 3 deaths overnight
item.description:
Health officials on Wednesday said they recorded 534 fresh cases of dengue onslaughts killing at least three persons in the past 24 hours.
"During the period, (of the 534) 68 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 71 in Chittagong division, 131 in Dhaka division, 56 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 65 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 45 in Khulna division, 37 in Mymensingh division, 30 in Rajshahi division, 26 in Rangpur division and five in Sylhet division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.
Since the start of the dengue onslaughts, Bangladesh this year has witnessed so far 50 deaths while the disease inflicted 14,690.
Last year, dengue claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country.
Besides, dengue claimed 575 lives and inflicted 1,01,214 people in 2024.

item.title: PM meets Tahsin, who lost sister in Milestone tragedy
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday met Tahsin Abdullah, a schoolboy whose heartwarming smile at the closing ceremony of the Notun Kuri Sports 2025-26 touched millions, a year after the boy lost his elder sister in the Milestone School fighter jet crash.
Learning the heartbreaking story behind the widely shared photograph of the smiling boy on social media, the prime minister met Tahsin and his father Nazmul Haque at the prime minister's office at Bangladesh Secretariat on Wednesday, said PM’s Assistant Press Secretary Gazi Shahriar Pamir.
A photograph of Tahsin during the closing ceremony of the “Notun Kuri Sports 2025-26” at Bangladesh Army Stadium in the capital on July 27 went viral on social media, showing Tahsin in his school uniform stretching out both hands towards the prime minister with an expression of pure joy. But behind that heartwarming smile was a story of deep personal grief.
In July 2025, Tahsin lost his elder sister Tasnia in the tragic fighter jet crash at Milestone School in Uttara. Although both siblings studied at the same school, they were in separate buildings on that fateful day. Tahsin was then a sixth-grade student, while Tasnia was an eighth-grader. The fighter jet crashed into the building where Tasnia was attending classes.
Hearing the deafening explosion, young Tahsin rushed to find his elder sister. After hearing that saline and water were needed, he stood waiting with bottles of saline and water in his small hands for his sister. But that wait never ended.
According to his family, the tragedy changed Tahsin completely. During a healing session after the incident, he wrote: “I am in great pain. I have lost my beloved sister. She died. I miss her so, so much. She was my best friend.”
Since losing his sister, Tahsin's once cheerful and lively smile was rarely seen. But on July 27 was a different day. At the Bangladesh Army Stadium, as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was moving around the field during the closing ceremony, Tahsin became overwhelmed with joy when the prime minister came near him.
His innocent smile and excitement were captured on camera, and the photograph later spread widely on social media, with many people connecting emotionally with the boy’s happiness.
Later, the prime minister came to know that behind the smiling face in the photograph was a heartbreaking family history. After learning the details, he directed his Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon to take steps to inquire about Tahsin and his family.
As Tahsin arrived at prime minister’s office, the prime minister enquired about Tahsin's studies and ambitions. Tahsin said he wanted to become a successful businessman and do something that would benefit people and attract them.
The prime minister appreciated his dream and advised the young boy to concentrate on his studies, play sports regularly and work with sincerity and dedication to achieve his goals, Pamir said.
During the conversation, Tahsin said football was his favorite sports. The prime minister gifted him a basketball bearing his autograph and a drone set.
After the meeting, an excited Tahsin said he was very happy to meet the prime minister again. He said he never imagined he would get such an opportunity and described the entire experience as a complete surprise. He said he was eagerly waiting to go to school and share the story of meeting the prime minister with his friends.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also expressed deep sympathy and condolence to Tahsin’s father over the tragic loss of his daughter in the Milestone fighter jet crash.
PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon, Private Secretary-2 Md Mehedul Islam, Assistant Private Secretary-2 Abdur Rahman Sani, Associate Professor (Orthopedics) Dr Shah Muhammad Aman Ullah, Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony and Amra BNP Poribar Member Secretary Moksedul Momin Mithun were present.

India lower house passes bill raising penalties for exam leaks
item.description:
India’s lower house of parliament approved a bill on Wednesday that would toughen penalties for leaking exam papers, after youth-led protests calling for sweeping reforms forced the education minister to resign.
The legislation would double the maximum jail term for those involved in leaking exam papers to 10 years, and raises the maximum fine to more than $1 million.
Lawmakers approved the bill by a voice vote after a raucous, hours-long debate, according to India’s public broadcaster.
It will next be put to a vote in the upper house, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling alliance holds a majority. Modi’s cabinet greenlighted the stricter punishments last week.
The approval follows weeks of mass protests over leaked exam papers and other irregularities, which culminated in the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday.
The protests, spearheaded by the online Cockroach Janta Party movement, drew massive support from students across the country and presented a major challenge to Modi’s government.
Rahul Gandhi of the main opposition Congress Party said he could relate to the frustration among India’s youth over the country’s education system.
“This was not anger... this was not hatred, this was deep expression of the youth of this country, of the future generation of this country, and I feel that all political parties must respect this expression,” he said in a speech in the house.
Despite rapid economic growth in the world’s most populous country, millions of young people face a shortage of well-paid jobs and fierce competition for careers.
The intense pressure to succeed has fueled a vast network of coaching centers and created opportunities for criminal groups to profit by selling leaked exam questions.
Despite repeated government crackdowns, such leaks have remained a recurring problem in both national and state-level examinations.
Demonstrations against the paper leaks in New Delhi turned violent on July 20 when huge crowds attempted to march towards parliament from the Jantar Mantar protest site.
Police fired tear gas and used batons to disperse the protest, triggering clashes and a wave of detentions.

item.title: France expands mass evacuations as Spain battles wildfires
item.description:
As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France carried out one of Europe’s biggest evacuations since World War II, scientists warned that extreme wildfires are becoming more frequent worldwide.
On Tuesday, French authorities evacuated another 4,000 people from Atlantic coast resorts adding to the 220,000 other people fleeing a blazing wildfire in southwest France.
Fresh fires broke out near the Atlantic resort of Grand Crohot west of Bordeaux, prompting authorities to deploy 23 planes and helicopters to contain the flames.
“The situation remains complicated. We’re not out of the woods,” said Sophie Brocas, the top government official in the coastal region of Gironde, where Grand Crohot and Bordeaux are located.
The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.
In Spain, there was a respite for the evacuees as thousands of residents were allowed to return home after firefighters managed to contain major blazes.
However, authorities remained on alert for a fourth summer heatwave with temperatures expected to exceed 40 degrees Celsius on Wednesday.
The biggest concern for firefighters in Spain was two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills to the west of Madrid.
In Avila, to the northwest of Madrid, a pyrocumulonimbus cloud was seen over the blaze. Scientists describe these clouds as fire-generated thunderstorms forming over intense heat sources like wildfires or volcanic eruptions.
“We are feeling a lot of anger and helplessness. It’s something inhuman,” 48-year-old gardener David Gonzalez said about the destruction caused by the fires in Avila.
Experts fear that incoming heat waves might cause the blazing fires to worsen.

Russian fencer wins world championship gold under his country flag
item.description:
A Russian has won a gold medal at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, the first since the country was allowed to compete again under its own flag in the combat sport.
Pavel Graudyn, 19, defeated South Korean Do Gyeong-dong 15-7 in the men's individual sabre final on Tuesday, having earlier stunned France's top-seed Sebastien Patrice in the last 16.
It was the first major championship since the International Fencing Federation (FIE) lifted all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2.
The sanctions had been imposed in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine and consequent war, with Russian and Belarusian fencers allowed to participate only as neutrals.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) earlier this month lifted some restrictions allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in team events and qualifying for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
Ukraine slammed the IOC decision as "premature" and "unfounded" after more than four years of conflict since Russia's invasion.
Governing bodies for swimming, gymnastics, judo, taekwondo and wrestling have also recently lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes.

item.title: FIFA's plans to sell $4.2bn stake in its tournaments widely criticised
item.description:
CONCACAF and AFC followed UEFA on Wednesday by criticising FIFA's controversial plans to sell a stake in the business operations of the World Cup and its other competitions through the creation of a semi-private subsidiary.
World football's governing body said Tuesday it would retain a majority share in FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) but hoped to raise $4.2 billion later this year by "carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests".
FIFA's statement was a rapid response to a story in British newspapers The Times and The Financial Times based on leaks of the plan from two sources.
The Times reported that FIFA president Gianni Infantino, 56, stood to profit from the scheme by becoming commissioner of the FFE after his expected next term expires in 2031. FIFA denied that this had been discussed.
The article also said discussion had started with financial advisors and potential investors.
Those include Thrive capital, an investment company founded and led by Joshua Kushner, brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, as well as an arm of JP Morgan Chase, the US bank that attempted to finance the failed breakaway European Super League.
European football's governing body UEFA, which has been critical of Infantino, responded to the reports before FIFA had even made an announcement.
"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross. UEFA takes it extremely seriously," said UEFA's statement.
"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade -- especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."
The European Union made no bones about their disdain for the plan.
"Hands off our game," Glenn Micallef, the EU commissioner for Sport, posted on X.
CONCACAF, which governs North and Central American football, said it was "deeply concerned by the lack of due process".
"We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place," CONCACAF added.
The plan would still have to be approved by the 38-member FIFA council and the majority of its 211 member associations (MAs). FIFA said it intends to present the plans to the council soon.
FIFA said in its statement that it "would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions".
It said it believed FFE would achieve an "initial equity valuation of $20bn".
FIFA said each of its MAs would be given the chance to take a one-off stake of 20mn dollars in FFE.
That represents only 0.1 percent of the total, but would be a significant sum for the leaderships of FIFA's poorer or smaller members.
"Together with other existing FIFA programmes, these investments could bring FIFA's total planned development funding to more than $10 billion over the next four years," FIFA said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, an Everton fan, decried the plan.
"Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine," he wrote on social media.
"The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell."
In June, ahead of the World Cup, FIFA, which folds competition income into revenue for the whole year, anticipated record revenues exceeding seven billion euros ($8bn) for 2026.
It was the first World Cup with 48 teams. At the start, Infantino said "we have had discussions about expanding to 64 teams" for 2030.
The Times quoted an unnamed "senior football figure" calling the plan "potentially much worse than the European Super League", as it would have an impact on all levels of football across the globe.
In 2019, a FIFA stakeholders' committee rejected an Infantino-backed plan for a $25bn private investment in an expanded Club World Cup. Reported backers included SoftBank of Japan and Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.
FIFA did expand that competition from seven teams to 32 clubs in 2025.
The Times speculated that the creation of FFE could have an impact on the World Cup and the Club World Cup.
"It could lead to pressure for both events to be further expanded or played more regularly than the present once every four years," it wrote.
FIFA has previously found itself in trouble with deals spinning off commercial activities to private partners.

Apparel leaders want to source gas from CNG stations amid severe shortage
item.description:
Amid a severe gas shortage triggered by the shutdown of a Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) terminal in Maheshkhali, the country's two leading apparel trade bodies—the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA)—have urged the government to allow export-oriented garment factories to source Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) in cylinders from filling stations.
In separate letters issued on July 28, the trade associations informed the government that granting factories temporary access to CNG stations until regular gas supplies normalize would help maintain production and export operations.
The appeal follows an order issued on July 27 by Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company, which directed all CNG filling stations to immediately stop selling natural gas in open cylinders or gas cascades to non-authorized vehicles.
Titas stated that such supplies pose severe safety risks and violate the Gas Act 2010 and the Gas Distribution Rules 2026.
Titas warned in its letter that supplying gas in unauthorized cylinders is illegal and highly dangerous, adding that non-compliance could lead to connection disconnections and legal action.
In a letter sent to the President of the Bangladesh CNG Filling Station and Conversion Workshop Owners Association, BGMEA president Mahmud Hasan Khan stated that the readymade garment sector is the primary engine of the national economy, driving maximum export earnings, generating millions of jobs, and earning foreign exchange.
He noted that the shutdown of one of the two FSRU LNG terminals in Maheshkhali has caused a severe gas crisis across industrial hubs. Gas pressure in many factories has dropped to zero PSI, making it increasingly difficult to sustain production and deliver shipments to international buyers on schedule.
The BGMEA requested that factories with urgent operational needs be granted temporary permission to collect gas in cylinders from CNG filling stations to safeguard production and honor export commitments.
The association added that Titas's recent order has made many filling stations reluctant to supply gas in cylinders.
BKMEA seeks ministry intervention
Meanwhile, in a notice to its members, the BKMEA stated that following Titas's directive, the association's president discussed the matter with the Secretary of the Energy and Mineral Resources Division.
According to BKMEA, after explaining that disruptions to gas supply in export-oriented industries would severely harm production and exports, the Energy Secretary instructed Titas's managing director to take necessary measures so that export-oriented factories can continue sourcing gas from CNG filling stations as before.
The trade body advised member factories to strictly adhere to government regulations and safety guidelines while collecting gas, and urged those with alternative LMG (mobile gas) setups to utilize them at full capacity.
The BKMEA noted that the current gas shortage may persist until August 8, after which conditions are expected to gradually normalize. It added that it remains in regular contact with relevant authorities to monitor the situation.

Through this partnership, we are bringing them a dedicated set of banking privileges designed around their unique professional journey and financial needs.”

item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami on Wednesday demanded that the Election Commission withdraw its proposed provision barring MPO-listed teachers from contesting local government elections and cancel the contractual appointment of an additional secretary over “political affiliation”.
A six-member Jamaat delegation, led by its Secretary General Mia Golam Parwar, sat in a meeting with Chief Election Commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin at the Nirbachan Bhaban in Dhaka's Agargaon and submitted a letter to the CEC.
Election Commissioners Abdur Rahmanel Masud and Tahmida Ahmad, along with EC Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed, were also present at the meeting in the morning.
According to a letter submitted to the CEC, Jamaat also demanded consideration of its previous opinions regarding the local government election code of conduct, which were placed before the Election Commission on June 30 last.
In the letter, Jamaat said the EC has sent a proposal to the Ministry of Local Government declaring MPO-affiliated teachers ineligible to contest in local government elections.
If the proposed provision is implemented, several lakhs of teachers and employees of more than 30,000 MPO-affiliated educational institutions in the country will be deprived of the opportunity to participate in local government elections, which is inconsistent with the principles of equality and non-discrimination enshrined in Articles 27 and 28 of the Constitution, it added.
“So, we believe that the proposed provision needs to be reconsidered and withdrawn or amended so that the constitutional right of eligible citizens to political participation remains intact,” it said.
Jamaat also demanded the immediate cancellation of the recent contractual appointment of 67-year-old Md Shamsul Alam as an additional secretary to the EC Secretariat, alleging that he had links with a political party.
The party claimed that media reports regarding his alleged political affiliation have raised questions among people about the neutrality of the Election Commission.
The Jamaat delegation also included Assistant Secretaries General Dr AHM Hamidur Rahman Azad, Ahsanul Mahboob Zubair and Moazzem Hossain Helal, members of its central working committee Jasim Uddin Sarkar and Shishir Mohammad Monir.

What freedom is and is not
item.description:
In an era of rising authoritarianism, democratic backsliding, and governments across the world wrapping repression in the language of liberty, On Freedom (Crown, 2024) by historian Timothy Snyder is a passionate plea to uphold freedom as the foundation of all political activity. To him, freedom is not a value to be chanted but rather a series of activities that ensure the realization of potential inherent to every human being. His focus in this book is distinguishing negative freedom, or freedom from, from positive freedom, or freedom to.
Negative freedom is a conception of freedom that defines freedom as the removal of certain obstacles only—which can be race, ethnicity, class, or a colonizer. Snyder gives the example of the colonized states, which failed to recognize that breaking free from the colonizers was only the beginning of their struggle. Positive freedom, on the other hand, is recognizing that freedom is always freedom to do activities that are essential to ensure that freedom is for everyone. Positive freedom is the route to make freedom available for everyone, not a select few with state or corporate power. Snyder puts forward five forms of this freedom—sovereignty, unpredictability, mobility, factuality, and solidarity.
The first chapter is on sovereignty. Snyder introduces two terms, which he recounts throughout the book—Leib and Körper. The former means a living body, where "living" includes the ability to govern itself, whereas "Körper" means just a body, subject to physical laws. Snyder brings up the Covid-19 vaccine crisis, where big pharmaceuticals treated the bodies of the victims as Körper to profit, not Leib to save. This fundamental empathy of treating oneself as a sovereign Leib and treating others as such is being free.
Unpredictability, the second form, is perhaps the most counterintuitive. Being unpredictable means being creative, recognizing the differences within humans while being cooperative. He encourages his readers to be unpredictable, to not be led by political demagogues and social media, but rather to appreciate creativity and the realization of new values through multiple combinations of them.
The third form is mobility. This part focuses on the state’s role in creating opportunities for its citizens. Mobility was the crux of the American Dream, and it was largely a result of Roosevelt’s New Deal and other social and economic programs to facilitate it. But in the Reagan era, these rights were overturned, with Reagan arguing that “the state” was the obstacle to freedom. In practice, these meant freedom only for oligarchs. To build freedom for everyone, social mobility is essential. Without social mobility, one cannot be sovereign or unpredictable—they have to be suppressed either under the state or the so-called free market, and that is unfreedom.
Factuality, the fourth form, takes on particular urgency in an era of conspiracy theories, AI-generated misinformation, and climate change denialism. Snyder's argument is that historically, freedom of speech was about speaking truth to power and protecting the people who spoke truth to power, and it should be exercised with responsibility to be scientific and fact-based.
Lastly, he discusses solidarity as a form of freedom, because no one is actually free while others are unfree. Without solidarity, divisions are inevitable, and they collectively reduce everyone’s freedom. Therefore, Snyder remarks, an individual cannot be free on his own—they needs structures that have been built by previous generations and the support of others who take care of them.
The book closes with a warning directed at democracies that perform the aesthetics of freedom while institutionalizing its opposite. For Bangladesh and Syria, countries that have recently removed authoritarian governments, this is not an abstract concern. Snyder's message is pointed: removing a dictator is negative freedom. What comes after, the slow, collective, continuous work of building institutions that make freedom real for everyone, is where the harder struggle begins.
On Freedom is not without its gaps. Snyder's focus on the American and European experience means the Global South appears mostly as illustration rather than subject. Readers in Dhaka will find the framework useful but will need to do their own work applying it to a political context Snyder does not fully reckon with. That is a limitation worth naming. But the book's core argument—that freedom is a practice, not a possession, and that it requires structures, solidarity, and honesty to survive—is one that travels.
Sadman Ahmed Siam is a student at the Islamic University of Technology.

item.title: The meme thief
item.description:
The boy’s name is Rafiq, though hardly anyone remembers it anymore. Online he goes by Bhoot Jolokia, a name borrowed from the world’s hottest chili. His followers call him Bhoot for short, half in awe, half in fear. By day, he is just another Dhaka University student struggling to stretch his money across rising food prices, hostel rent, and never-ending load-shedding. By night, though, his phone becomes a factory of laughter and fire.
Rafiq’s tiny room in a peeling dormitory smells of damp clothes and stale Singara wrappers. A fan rattles above him like an old tin can in the wind. Outside, the traffic roars endlessly down Nilkhet Road. But on his cracked phone screen, the world bends to his humor. He lifts screenshots of political speeches, photos of overpaid cricketers, and stills of ministers cutting ribbons at useless “inaugurations.” With a flick of his thumbs, captions bloom like thorns:
“Dhaka Metro Rail: Motijheel to Kamalapur, 1000 crores gone. Slow and steady robs the race.”
“Minister says onions are cheaper this year. My tears disagree.”
Within minutes, thousands of people share his posts. People from all walks of life scroll through their Android phones during lunch breaks and laugh at them. Even private university students in Bashundhara whisper the memes like they’re contraband jokes. His humor does what no slogan or rally can: it slips past fear.
But Rafiq knows the danger. Satire in Bangladesh walks a knife’s edge. In his childhood, he had heard stories of editors jailed for cartoons and writers harassed for tweets. He remembers the silence after the Holey Artisan attack, when everyone feared words could turn fatal.
Still, he continues. He tells himself he is not a revolutionary. He is a trickster—slippery and ambiguous. If the king dislikes the joke, he can always say, “It was just chili, bhai. Don’t take it so seriously.”
One evening in September, a storm batters Dhaka. Rainwater gushes over the sidewalks, carrying plastic cups and dead rats toward the Buriganga. The power dies, plunging Rafiq’s room into a cave-like dark. He lights a single candle and stares at the latest headline: Parliament approves “Digital Security Act 2.0.”
He laughs bitterly. “Security for whom?” he mutters. Then he crafts a meme:
A minister smiling broadly, the caption—
“New Digital Act: Because laughter is the real national threat.”
He posts it without thinking. The screen glowed briefly before the signal disappeared into the storm.
The next morning, his phone explodes with shares, comments, warnings. "Bro, be careful,” one follower messages. Another writes, “They’ll knock at your door.”
By noon, the meme is on the lips of tea-stall owners at Shahbagh and students marching in New Market. Rafiq watches with a mixture of pride and dread. The trickster has slipped too close to the tiger’s tail.
Two days later, the knock comes.
It is not a violent pounding but a polite tok-tok at the dormitory door. Rafiq opens to find two men in plain clothes, faces expressionless. “We need to talk,” one says. His voice is calm, almost friendly.
They take him to a tea stall instead of a station. One stirs his tea absentmindedly and says, “You are talented. Why waste your time on these dangerous jokes? We can arrange a proper job for you. Design social media campaigns. Earn respect.”
The other adds more sternly, “Stop playing with fire, brother. Jokes can turn into mobs. And mobs—into crimes.”
Rafiq listens, nodding. He said he would think about it. They leave him with a phone number scrawled on tissue paper.
That night, he cannot sleep. He stared at the candle again, thinking of Gopal Bhar—the court jester who survived by laughing with kings, not against them. Was he foolish to resist? Should he accept the offer and sell his wit for comfort?
But then he remembers a message from a clerk at a bank he once met online: “Bhai, your memes make my 10-hour day lighter. Don’t stop.”
The trickster inside him grins. If the king is laughing, the trickster has failed.
So Rafiq begins a new game. He hides his satire inside layers of absurdity.
He posts a photo of a giant Hilsa fish and writes: “Breaking News: Hilsa appointed minister of finance. Experts say it’s the most transparent minister yet.”
He shares an edited video where a politician’s speech is interrupted by a cow mooing.
He invents a character called Baba Onionswami, a mystical guru who predicts inflation by staring at vegetable baskets.
The officials could not decide if these posts were mockery or nonsense. The people, though, understood. The laughter grows sharper, louder, impossible to contain.
One afternoon, while sipping tea at DU Canteen, Rafiq overhears a group of law students analyzing one of his memes as if it were a text in class.
“This one,” a bespectacled boy says, “uses parody to dismantle the state narrative.”
Another adds, “It’s like Bakhtin’s carnival—the inversion of authority through humor.”
Rafiq nearly choked on his tea. He never intended to theory. His memes were like chili—burning quick and crude. But maybe chili, too, could be philosophy.
Then comes December, Victory Day. Dhaka is drenched in green and red. Rafiq creates his boldest meme yet: a photoshopped image of the National Parliament building floating like a boat in floodwater, with the caption—
“Fifty years of independence: Still trying to stay afloat.”
It spreads like wildfire. Some call it art; others call it treason. By evening, TV talk shows debated its meaning.
And then—just as suddenly—it vanishes. Facebook deleted it. His account was locked. Bhoot Jolokia was erased.
For a week, silence. Rafiq walks Dhaka’s streets feeling invisible. He is just another student again, lost in the crowd.
But then, one morning at Nilkhet, he notices a poster on a wall. It shows the Parliament-boat meme, hand-drawn in marker, and the chili logo scrawled at the corner. Beside it, someone has written, "Bhoot lives.”
He walks further. More walls, more posters. Rickshaw hoods painted with chili signs. University bathroom doors scribbled with his jokes. His memes have escaped the phone, growing wilder in the city’s veins.
The trickster could not be caught, he realized. The trickster is never just one person.
Haroonuzzaman is a Bangladeshi translator, novelist, poet, researcher, and academic.

item.title: 5 Bangladeshi women return home after serving jail terms in India
item.description:
Five Bangladeshi women returned home through Benapole land port on Tuesday night after serving jail terms in India.
Petrapole immigration police handed them over to Benapole immigration police around 8pm under special travel permits.
The returnees were Papia Akter, Shimu Akter, Sharmin Khatun, Lovely Khatun and Rozina Khatun. They are from Jessore, Narail, Bagerhat and Tangail districts.

item.title: Over 53.94% of Khulna primary schools running without head teachers
item.description:
More than half of the government primary schools in Khulna Division are operating without head teachers, creating challenges for academic management and administrative activities.
Of the division’s 8,165 government primary schools, 4,405 have vacant head teacher posts, meaning 53.94% of schools do not have permanent heads, according to the Primary Education Directorate.
Among these schools, 1,348 are currently being managed by assistant teachers serving as acting head teachers.
Md Shariful Islam, deputy director of primary education in Khulna Division, said the shortage exists across all 10 districts of the division.
“Of the total schools, 4,405 have vacant head teacher posts,” he said.
The number of schools without head teachers is 605 in Khulna, 672 in Bagerhat, 468 in Satkhira, 691 in Jashore, 523 in Jhenaidah, 271 in Magura, 415 in Kushtia, 287 in Chuadanga, 320 in Narail and 153 in Meherpur.
Assistant teachers are performing acting head teacher duties in 1,348 schools, including 301 in Jessore, 255 in Satkhira, 188 in Bagerhat and 131 in Khulna.
Khulna District Primary Education Officer Sheikh Ahidul Alam said 605 out of 1,159 government primary schools in the district are without head teachers.
The highest number of vacancies is in Dumuria, where 113 schools have no head teacher, followed by Koyra with 85 schools and Paikgachha with 73 schools.
Other affected areas include Khulna Sadar with 56 schools, Dakop 55, Batiaghata 52, Rupsha 37, Phultala 39, Terokhada 62 and Dighalia 33.
Sheikh Ahidul Alam said documents for promoting eligible assistant teachers to head teacher positions have already been sent to the Directorate of Primary Education.
“Once the recruitment and promotion process is completed through the Bangladesh Public Service Commission and the Directorate, the vacant posts can gradually be filled,” he said.
He added that around 300 schools in Khulna were assigned acting head teachers in 2018, but the number has declined due to retirement and death of teachers.
Koyra upazila is among the worst affected areas, with 85 out of 142 government primary schools operating without head teachers.
According to the upazila primary education office, these schools have 22,806 students.
Officials said no head teacher has been appointed to any primary school in Koyra since 2013.
Several schools, including Gobra Ghatakhali Government Primary School, Uttar Madinabad Government Primary School, Swarnakali Government Primary School and Srirampur Government Primary School, are currently without permanent heads.
The upazila also has 42 vacant assistant teacher posts.
Habibur Rahman, a resident of Gobra village whose son studies at Gobra Ghatakhali Government Primary School, said the absence of a head teacher has affected academic activities.
“Teaching has been disrupted. A permanent head teacher should be appointed soon to improve the learning environment,” he said.
Acting head teachers said managing both classroom teaching and administrative responsibilities has become increasingly difficult.
They said preparing official reports, maintaining records, handling accounts and implementing government instructions often leave them with less time for teaching.
Md Billal Hossain, acting head teacher of Gobra Ghatakhali Government Primary School, has been performing the additional responsibility since 2023.
The school has 157 students and five assistant teachers, including him.
“Appointing a permanent head teacher would help improve the overall management of the school,” he said.
Officials said legal complications are also contributing to the prolonged vacancies.
Nurul Amin, acting head teacher of Swarnakali Government Primary School, said a case over the status and ranking of teachers from 10 schools that were brought under government management is still pending.
He said the unresolved case has created uncertainty over promotions and postings of teachers from those schools.
Students of Shyamnagar Government Primary School said some teachers cannot take regular classes as they are engaged in additional administrative duties.
The Koyra Upazila Primary Education Office is also facing manpower shortages.
Three of the five posts of assistant upazila education officers are vacant, while all four office assistant positions have remained unfilled for a long time.
Koyra Upazila Primary Education Officer Tapan Kumar Karmakar said acting responsibilities have been assigned to assistant teachers for 16 vacant head teacher posts.
He said steps have been taken to fill some positions, but legal complications have delayed the process.

item.title: It turns people into animals: Bangladesh’s growing yaba addiction crisis
item.description:
“Metalfreak” once spent hours caring for his pet bird every day, stroking her, cleaning her cage and letting her fly freely. Now, he says, he cannot even bring himself to do that. “Who cares?” he says, lying on his bed in his cluttered Dhaka bedroom.
The man in his forties, who asked to go by his chosen pseudonym, has an increasingly debilitating addiction to yaba, a drug mixing methamphetamine and caffeine, which is destroying lives in Bangladesh.
Yaba, which means “crazy medicine” in Thai, is thought to be used by millions of Bangladeshis, with numbers continuing to rise.
To consume it, Metalfreak puts a pill on tinfoil and heats it from below, before inhaling the fumes. The impact of each of the orange pills lasts four to five hours, he says. He stays awake for three days at a time before crashing and sleeping for 12 hours or more.
In June, Bangladeshi home minister Salahuddin Ahmed said nearly 5 per cent of the country’s population of roughly 175 million people have a drug addiction, and “the emergence of new synthetic and semi-synthetic drugs” was “further intensifying the problem,” according to local media. This month Bangladesh’s parliament approved a Bill retaining the death penalty for some drugs-related offences.
Yaba is considered a class-A banned substance in Bangladesh. In 2018, under ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina, there was a crackdown by authorities, with more than 200 people killed in a few months in behaviour reminiscent of Filipino president Rodrigo Duterte’s brutal “war on drugs”.
The killings have led to concerned pronouncements by the EU and the UN high commissioner for human rights. Amnesty International has said 466 people were killed in 2018, saying what was presented as an anti-drugs campaign “spread terror in some of the country’s poorest neighbourhoods, where people fear the slightest suspicion of being involved in drug abuse may lead to their loved ones being subjected to another alleged extrajudicial execution”. Tens of thousands more were arrested, reports the Irish Times.
Yet usage continues to rise, local experts say. “If we want to reduce substance use, we have to improve mental health services,” says Dr Md Arifuzzaman, a registrar at the National Institute of Mental Health, who also works at Niramoy rehabilitation centre in Dhaka. “Life is waiting where recovery begins” is written on the wall behind its reception.
There are about 350 psychiatrists in the whole country, he says. In the National Institute, psychiatrists might see 20 patients in one hour, “but we have no other option”. He says there is a similar lack of qualified psychologists in Bangladesh. He wants the government to integrate mental health into primary healthcare. Bangladesh’s last national mental health survey, carried out in 2018-2019, found that about 90 per cent of people who need mental healthcare do not seek treatment. Arifuzzaman says stigma around mental health is “prevailing all over the world, in our country as well,” but in the past few years awareness has increased a “magnificent amount”.
Yaba addiction is “very common”, though many users use other drugs too, which could include buprenorphine injections, heroin, and omorphone tablets, he says. Almost every substance is increasing in use, with yaba usage “significantly increasing.”
He says some users remain “functional”, while others have “vulnerabilities in the brain” that mean they will be more affected. Certain external events – such as crises related to flooding, fires and the Covid-19 pandemic can also trigger the situation.
Arifuzzaman says some users become dealers because they have no other way to support their habit. Some users were originally dealing with mental conditions, such as depression, anxiety disorders or psychosis, and were seeking relief when they turned to drugs.
The availability of substances clearly plays a role in which drugs are commonly taken, Arifuzzaman says. Yaba was traditionally used in parts of Asia by occupational workers such as truck drivers, before shifting into “youth culture” in the late 1990s, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. In 2007, 1.2 million tablets were confiscated in Bangladesh, the body said.
The area where Thailand, Myanmar and Laos meet, known as the Golden Triangle, is believed to be one of the world’s most active areas for the production of synthetic drugs. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime says a record 236 tonnes of methamphetamine (commonly known as meth) were seized in east and southeast Asia in 2024, a 24 per cent increase on 2023, with much more likely going on sale. Myanmar is believed to be the main producer of the yaba in Bangladesh.
“Everyone has the same sob story,” says Metalfreak. He says Bangladeshis who become addicted to yaba usually start with cigarettes, then weed, then cough syrup. As a young man, he was familiar with “downers” such as cannabis. The first time he took yaba he was expecting it would be good to “hang, chill” but it “put my mind through the roof ... This thing makes people animal.”
Yaba used to be more expensive. Now there are two categories of the drug available: cheap and expensive. The cheaper versions “totally f**k” your mouth and teeth, he says, while “you can see in [a user’s] eyes they’re crazy.” Metalfreak says he has lost friends to these pills – taking it consistently can lead to a stroke, he says. Others lose teeth or start “twitching”.
In the past few years, it has become harder to get opium or heroin, Metalfreak says. Yaba “totally kicked out all other drugs”. In Dhaka it is easy to spot young people selling packets of the pills on the street. In an area called Mohammadpur, young boys hold up sachets of the pills while rickshaw drivers reach to take them.
Bangladesh has experienced political instability in recent years. As many as 1,400 people are thought to have been killed during 2024 protests that led to Hasina’s ousting, before a 2026 election led to a victory for the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, led by Tarique Rahman. Classified as a lower-middle-income country by the World Bank, the south Asian country has also been assessed as particularly vulnerable to climate change by various global rankings. Many young people worry about their future.
All of this upheaval has personal implications. Metalfreak’s father, who recently died, was lauded as a freedom fighter, he says, but more recently friends dismiss him as a “fraud”. Metalfreak ran a business, but the premises burnt down in a type of fire that seems surprisingly common in Bangladesh – he thinks it was done on purpose, though others say it could have been an electrical fault or another type of accident.
When he engages with the world now, it is through Instagram, where he watches endless videos about Gaza. Brown people and Muslims in particular are treated as worthless globally, he says, adding that he has despaired at the western media and the US.
Metalfreak says yaba gives people “false confidence”, with many believing “weird conspiracy theories”. His conversation meanders, veering into thoughts on Kim Jong-un, Uyghurs in China, Kneecap, Venezuela, Aung San Suu Kyi and Vladimir Putin.
Metalfreak says the economic situation influences everything in Bangladesh – terrorism, crime and addiction. He thinks better-off people are the ones with time to develop addictions. “I’m privileged ... I have a room. I can lie down. I don’t have to think tomorrow: about who’s going feed me, feed my family.”
He worries about the impact of the drugs: how yaba users “will never last two years” because they don’t sleep. “It’s a slow poisoning, it’s a meticulous plan.”

The Prime Minister stressed the need to reduce traffic congestion during school opening and closing hours, noting that unmanaged parking in front of educational institutions often contributes to gridlock.
He suggested that a portion of school grounds could be used for parking to help ease congestion.
Local Government Division Secretary Shahidul Hasan, Rajuk Chairman Engineer Riazul Islam, Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Abdus Salam, Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqur Rahman Khan, DMP Acting Commissioner Md Sarwar and DIG (Traffic) Anisur Rahman were present.

item.description:
Social Welfare Minister Dr AZM Zahid Hossain on Tuesday said if advanced treatment for hepatitis B can be ensured within the country, it will reduce patients' tendency to travel abroad for treatment as well as cut medical costs.
“The country's healthcare system needs to acquire modern technology and international expertise to move forward,” the minister made these remarks at a programme organized by the Gastroenterology Society of Bangladesh at Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) to mark World Hepatitis Day.
This year's theme for the day is "Elimination for Everyone, Everywhere, Right Now."
Minister Zahid said a significant section of Bangladesh's population is suffering from fatty liver disease without being aware of it.
He said the number of fatty liver patients in the country is rising day by day due to excessive carbohydrate intake, and called upon all concerned to raise public awareness on the issue.
Referring to the appointment of Professor Simon Taylor-Robinson, emeritus professor of Hepatology at Imperial College London, to the Department of Hepatology at BMU, the minister said involving foreign and regional experts to evaluate students against international and regional standards would play an important role in improving the quality of medical education.
He urged other medical colleges to take similar timely initiatives.
At one point during the event, members of the Gastroenterology Society of Bangladesh demanded that hepatitis B screening be made mandatory for all pregnant women.
The minister termed the demand timely and assured full cooperation from his position to help implement it.
Professor Simon Taylor-Robinson presented the keynote paper at the event.

item.title: ULAB hosts workshop, cultural performance on Manipuri heritage
item.description:
The Department of General Education (GED) at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB), in collaboration with MAATRA Gobeshona Songstha, organized an academic workshop and cultural performance titled Manipuri Culture: Society, Festivals and Performing Arts as part of its Introduction to Drama course.
The event was held on Tuesday under the chairmanship of Professor Shahnaj Husne Jahan, head of the Department of General Education. Students, faculty members from different departments and invited guests attended the programme.
The academic session was conducted by Manipuri researcher Sukanta Sinha, who spoke on the history, cultural heritage, social life, festivals, music, dance traditions and artistic legacy of the Manipuri community. The session concluded with an interactive question-and-answer segment.
A highlight of the event was a live Pung (Manipuri drum) performance and a classical Manipuri dance recital by Arnab Sharma, adjunct faculty member of the Department of Dance at the University of Dhaka. His performance showcased the aesthetics, rhythm, spirituality and expressive traditions of Manipuri performing arts.
According to the organizers, the combination of academic discussion and live cultural performances provided students with an experiential learning opportunity while fostering a greater appreciation of Bangladesh’s cultural diversity and intangible cultural heritage.
ULAB and MAATRA Gobeshona Songstha said the initiative reflects their shared commitment to promoting indigenous knowledge, preserving cultural heritage, encouraging intercultural dialogue and enriching students’ learning through academic and cultural engagement.

item.title: BSTI advises against swallowing toothpaste amid microplastics debate
item.description:
The Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution (BSTI) has urged the public not to panic over a recent study that detected microplastics in several toothpaste brands sold in the country, advising consumers to maintain proper oral hygiene and avoid swallowing toothpaste.
In a press release issued on Tuesday, BSTI said no toothpaste brand or product should be declared unsafe or substandard before the findings are scientifically and legally verified.
The statement comes after the Environment and Social Development Organization (ESDO), a private research organisation, reported detecting microplastics in 26 of 34 toothpaste samples tested. BSTI said it is treating the findings with utmost importance because of their potential implications for public health and the environment.
According to BSTI, microplastics are plastic particles measuring 5 millimetres or less that are generally invisible to the bare eye. The World Health Organization (WHO said that microplastics are an emerging environmental and public health concern, although there is still no conclusive scientific evidence on their health risks. It stressed that further research is needed.
The press release also outlined international regulatory developments. It noted that the United States banned the intentional use of plastic microbeads in rinse-off cosmetic products, including toothpaste, under the Microbead-Free Waters Act in 2015. The European Union has given manufacturers until October 17, 2027, to phase out the use of intentionally added microplastics in such products.
However, BSTI said neither South Asian countries, including India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, nor international standards organisations have established a maximum permissible limit or a standard testing method for microplastics in toothpaste.
The agency said toothpaste manufacturers and importers in Bangladesh are required to obtain licences under BDS 1216:2012 Specification for Toothpaste before producing or marketing their products. Under government regulations, licences are issued only after products undergo chemical, microbiological and safety testing.
BSTI further said the country's approved list of 81 ingredients for toothpaste manufacturing does not include microplastics. It also evaluates manufacturers' quality control systems before granting licences, making the intentional use of microplastics unlikely.
The standards body stressed that the detection of plastic particles alone does not prove they were intentionally added by manufacturers or that they pose a risk to human health. Determining the particles' type, source, concentration and potential health risks requires further scientific analysis, it added.
As part of its review, BSTI has requested ESDO to provide the study's full report, testing methodology, raw data and other relevant documents. It is also collecting information from the manufacturers and importers concerned on raw materials, product ingredients and the use of synthetic polymers.

item.title: How to protect yourself from hepatitis
item.description:
Hepatitis B and C have emerged as major public health concerns in Bangladesh.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Bangladesh is among the 10 countries with the highest number of hepatitis C infections. However, timely vaccination, testing and treatment can prevent many cases and reduce complications.
Health experts say one of the biggest challenges is that people infected with viral hepatitis often show no symptoms for years. As a result, the disease is frequently diagnosed only after serious complications, such as liver cirrhosis or liver cancer, have developed.
WHO Representative to Bangladesh Dr Ahmed Jamsheed Mohamed said: “Hepatitis is preventable, treatable and, in the case of hepatitis C, curable. But many people develop severe complications because they do not receive timely testing and medical care.”
WHO recommends administering the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by all recommended doses, to provide the best protection.
Blood should always be screened for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and other infectious diseases before transfusion.
Always ensure that sterile syringes, needles and medical equipment are used for injections, dental procedures, tattoos and piercings. Reusing equipment significantly increases the risk of infection.
Avoid sharing razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers or any other items that may come into contact with blood.
Hepatitis B can spread through blood and bodily fluids. Practising safe sex helps reduce the risk of transmission.
People with a history of blood transfusions, a family history of hepatitis, healthcare workers and others at higher risk should undergo hepatitis B and C screening. Early diagnosis improves treatment outcomes.
Testing pregnant women for hepatitis B allows healthcare providers to take steps to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission.
Although hepatitis often causes no symptoms, seek medical advice if you experience jaundice, dark urine, persistent fatigue, loss of appetite or prolonged pain in the upper right side of the abdomen.
According to WHO, hepatitis B can be effectively managed with medication, while hepatitis C can be cured in most cases with modern antiviral drugs. Early treatment is crucial.
WHO says social stigma and misconceptions often discourage people from getting tested or treated. Raising awareness and supporting people living with hepatitis without discrimination are essential to controlling the disease.
Experts say the most effective tools against hepatitis are awareness, timely vaccination, regular screening of at-risk groups and prompt treatment. Expanding access to prevention and treatment services, along with strengthening the healthcare system and public awareness, could significantly reduce hepatitis-related deaths in Bangladesh.
